clue.text: Blitzed Londoners initially defiant, blown up

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word it follows
a blitzed thing has been bombed and scattered, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: the first letter of Londoners
taken as written

explanation.surface: Londoners during the Blitz stayed defiant even as their streets were bombed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blitzed' sits at the front looking like part of the wartime picture; it is the signal to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inflated has been filled with air, swollen like a balloon pumped full.

clue.text: Japanese drama about a conservationist

indicators.note: about means going around, so the drama's name wraps around the next piece

blocks.note: Noh is classical Japanese masked theatre
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Japanese play has an environmental campaigner as its subject.
explanation.walkthrough: Noh is the classical masked theatre of Japan; the single letter A goes inside it. Noah saved a pair of every species in the ark.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah preserved breeding pairs of every creature through the Flood, a humorous description of animal protection.

clue.text: Spectacles handled in the theatre

blocks.note: surface reading: shows or spectacles that are managed or staged in a theatre
setter's reading: eyeglasses fitted with a handle, used at the opera or theatre

explanation.surface: A director copes with the big stage shows in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spectacles' suggests stage shows and 'handled' suggests managing them; in fact these are glasses held up on a handle.
explanation.definitionFit: A lorgnette is a pair of glasses on a long handle, traditionally raised to the eyes at the opera.

clue.text: Performs without skill, producing loose ends

blocks.note: first meaning: strums an instrument idly and monotonously
second meaning: the fringe of unwoven warp threads left on a loom

explanation.surface: A clumsy musician's playing leaves things untidy and unfinished.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a weaving term: the leftover thread ends when cloth is cut from the loom.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrum is to strum aimlessly on strings, and thrums are short leftover yarn threads in weaving.

clue.text: Martini-Henry wasn't such a gun, in fact

blocks.note: surface reading: the Martini-Henry rifle was a single-shot weapon, not a twin-barrelled shotgun
setter's reading: yet its hyphenated two-part name is exactly the kind of surname described by the same phrase

explanation.surface: A note of military history: the Victorian Martini-Henry rifle had only one barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase describes both a shotgun with two barrels and a hyphenated surname, and Martini-Henry is a hyphenated name.
explanation.definitionFit: A shotgun with two barrels side by side is described this way, as is a hyphenated two-part surname.

clue.text: To make fools do it is wrong

indicators.note: wrong says the words are set out incorrectly, so their letters must be put in another order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A moral warning: making people look foolish is a wrong thing to do.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiots and fools are both plain synonyms for stupid people.

clue.text: Manufacturing enterprise showing diligence

blocks.note: first meaning: the making of goods in factories
second meaning: hard-working effort and application

explanation.surface: A factory business demonstrates how hard-working it is.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the production sector of an economy and the quality of working hard steadily.

clue.text: Playwright's one book three-quarters written

indicators.note: three-quarters of a four-letter word keeps three letters and drops the last

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
B is the abbreviation for book
a letter written is sent off

explanation.surface: A dramatist has one book that is three-quarters finished.
explanation.walkthrough: SENT loses its final quarter, the T. The 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian dramatist who wrote A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: Travel round by rail -- here today and gone tomorrow

blocks.note: transit is passage from place to place
the round shape of the letter O
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A train journey where you are in one place one day and elsewhere the next.
explanation.walkthrough: RY was the standard abbreviation for railway in old timetables and maps.
explanation.definitionFit: Something transitory is fleeting and short-lived, present briefly before vanishing.

clue.text: Rides here - just the place for it

blocks.note: just and fair both mean equitable
a ground is a site or place set aside for an activity

explanation.surface: Someone recommends a spot as ideal for going riding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rides' suggests horse riding; the rides meant are roundabouts and big wheels.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairground is the open space where carousels, dodgems and other amusement attractions are set up.

clue.text: Some of his acts were pleasant, others not

definitions.text: Some of his acts were pleasant, others not

blocks.clueFragment: Some of his acts were pleasant, others not
blocks.note: surface reading: a man whose behaviour was sometimes nice and sometimes nasty
setter's reading: acts are scenes of plays, and a dramatist published a collection called Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant

explanation.surface: A description of a man of mixed character, kind at some moments and nasty at others.
explanation.walkthrough: George Bernard Shaw published his early dramas in two volumes titled Plays Pleasant and Plays Unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: George Bernard Shaw, the Irish dramatist, grouped his early works under the titles Plays Pleasant and Unpleasant.

clue.text: Term reduced by head, lacking entitlement

blocks.note: a term is a name for something
reduced means made less
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A school term has been shortened by the headteacher, who had no right to do so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term' and 'head' suggest a school; head is a promontory, and 'entitlement' means having a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no title is having no name, so namelessness is the state of lacking any designation.

clue.text: Old car, for example, disposed of for another cycle

definitions.text: Old car, for example, disposed of for another cycle

blocks.clueFragment: Old car, for example, disposed of for another cycle
blocks.note: surface reading: someone gets rid of an old car and buys a bicycle instead
setter's reading: material thrown out to be recycled, a car being one example

explanation.surface: A motorist ditches the old banger and goes back to riding a bicycle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' looks like a bike, but the idea is recycling; an old car is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrap metal is discarded metal, such as a wrecked vehicle, sold to be melted down and reused.

clue.text: Second part of short tale heard

definitions.note: tale heard aloud is tail, so this is a short tail

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a cut is a share or portion

explanation.surface: A storyteller recites the second section of a brief story.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound change sits in the definition: a tale spoken sounds like a tail, and a scut is the short tail of a rabbit or deer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the stubby upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

clue.text: Outdoor pool used by divers?

blocks.note: surface reading: an open-air swimming pool where people practise diving
setter's reading: divers are also water birds, so this is a garden basin of water for birds

explanation.surface: An open-air swimming pool where people jump off the high board.
explanation.walkthrough: A diver is a kind of water bird (the loon), so the 'pool' is a garden basin for birds.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird-bath is a shallow garden basin of water where small birds drink and wash.

clue.text: Heavy artillery in Little Rock upset girl

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: the Rock is Gibraltar, and Gib is its shortened, little form
a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl in the Arkansas city of Little Rock is upset about heavy gunfire.
explanation.walkthrough: Little Rock looks like the American city; the Rock is Gibraltar, 'little' asks for its short form.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Bertha was the nickname of the huge German howitzer used in the First World War.

clue.text: They are held as securities by many over long periods

blocks.note: a host is a great number
ages are long stretches of time

explanation.surface: Financial bonds kept by many investors for years at a time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Securities' suggests stocks and bonds; here it means people held as guarantees. 'Over' places the first piece above the second in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Hostages are people seized and kept as a pledge that demands will be met.

clue.text: One who attends courses, often hoping for better luck

definitions.text: One who attends courses, often hoping for better luck

blocks.clueFragment: One who attends courses, often hoping for better luck
blocks.note: surface reading: a student who goes to classes and hopes to do better this time
setter's reading: courses are racecourses, where a punter hopes their bets come good

explanation.surface: A student keeps signing up for classes, hoping their fortunes improve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' suggests education; the courses are horse-racing tracks, and the luck is with the betting.
explanation.definitionFit: A racegoer is someone who attends horse races, usually placing bets on the runners.

clue.text: Surrounded, turning back, oddly

indicators.note: oddly asks for the letters in the odd positions only
back means the kept letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Someone encircled, turning round in a peculiar way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning back' reads as one phrase, but turning is the source word and back is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Girt is the old past tense of gird, meaning encircled or bound around.

clue.text: Form master to divide pupils into groups

indicators.note: to form is to shape or make, so the following letters are built into a new word

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A form master's job is to sort the pupils in a school class into sets.
explanation.walkthrough: A form master is a British teacher in charge of a class; here 'Form' is detached to signal rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Streaming is the school practice of placing pupils in separate classes according to ability.

clue.text: Scene of dramatic events that had spectators in tears, it is said

definitions.text: Scene of dramatic events that had spectators in tears, it is said

blocks.clueFragment: Scene of dramatic events that had spectators in tears
blocks.note: surface reading: a theatre where moving plays made the audience cry
setter's reading: spoken aloud, tears sounds like tiers, the stepped rows of seats around an arena

explanation.surface: A theatre where the tragedies were so moving the audience wept.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'it is said' asks you to hear tears as tiers; the seating rose in tiers around the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: An amphitheatre is an open arena ringed by banked rows of seats, used for plays and spectacles.

clue.text: Not all the wedding-cake is cut

indicators.note: not all of the phrase is used, only a run of letters from inside it

blocks.note: letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: At a reception, only part of the wedding cake gets sliced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' fits the cake perfectly, but it is the definition of a word for chopping, as with an axe.
explanation.definitionFit: To hew is to chop with an axe or blade, so hewed is a past tense of cut.

clue.text: Clock -- loud one

blocks.note: F is forte, the musical direction for loud
an ace is the one in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A noisy alarm clock, a particularly loud one.
explanation.walkthrough: Clock is British slang for a person's face, as well as the dial of a timepiece.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a clock is a person's face, and a clock's dial is also called its face.

clue.text: A dish from the fish-pond

blocks.note: first meaning: meat and vegetables cooked slowly in liquid
second meaning: an old word for a pond where fish are kept for the table

explanation.surface: A meal cooked from fish caught in a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is archaic: medieval monasteries kept stews, ponds stocked with fish to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a slow-cooked casserole and an archaic holding pond stocked with fish for eating.

clue.text: Whimsically humorous man taken in by heartless girl

indicators.note: heartless means the centre letter of the word is removed
taken in means swallowed or enclosed, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a girl's name
a man's name

explanation.surface: A funny man gets fooled by a cold-hearted girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken in' reads as deceived in the surface, but it means enclosed. The heart of a seven-letter name is its fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gilbertian humour is topsy-turvy and absurd, in the manner of W. S. Gilbert's comic opera librettos.

clue.text: She is a peeress in Gilbert & Sullivan

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: a peeress is a titled lady
the pair are known by their initials, G and S

explanation.surface: A trivia note about a noblewoman character in a Gilbert and Sullivan opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Peeresses do appear in Iolanthe, which makes the surface plausible; the definition is just 'She', a woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladys is a female first name, and the definition simply indicates some woman.

clue.text: Humiliated - indeed, you might say, abject

indicators.note: this asks for the preceding word to be split in a punning way, with its first two letters as an instruction to put something inside

blocks.note: split as 'in deed': the second word supplies these letters, the first is the instruction
abject and mean both describe something low and contemptible

explanation.surface: Someone was humiliated, made truly wretched and low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indeed' looks like a mere intensifier in the surface; the setter's 'you might say' is the hint to hear it as two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To be demeaned is to be lowered in dignity, which is what humiliation does.
